 An Austrian priest claims that 1.4 million Catholics are in lodges and not excommunicated
 Michael Heinrich Weninger, ordained by Schönborn, asks Rome to distinguish between regular and irregular lodges; the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith reiterated in 2023 that membership in Freemasonry is prohibited
 Masones con atuendos rituales durante una ceremonia, portando símbolos tradicionales como mandiles, espadas y bandas distintivas. 
 by InfoVaticana | 
 November 15, 2026 
 The Austrian priest Michael Heinrich Weninger , a former diplomat and author of a doctoral thesis in favor of reconciliation between the Church and Freemasonry, has once again called on Rome to change its stance. In a conference in Lübeck, reported by katholisch.de based on information from the portal Aussicht.online , Weninger estimated that around 1.4 million Catholics worldwide belong to a “genuine” lodge and maintained that, in his view, they are not excommunicated.
 According to the German Catholic portal, the priest argued that there is no fundamental contradiction between the Catholic faith and membership in regular Freemasonry, whose lodges require belief in God and prohibit political activity within their ranks. In his opinion, the Vatican still does not sufficiently distinguish between those lodges, which are religious in orientation, and openly anticlerical organizations. “Any madman can call himself a Mason” , he said. And he added: “A Mason is at heart a good person who works on himself to become even better” , to which, in his view, a Catholic priest has in principle nothing to object.
 Weninger also reviewed the history of modern Freemasonry, which he places at the feast of St. John in 1717, when what he called the mother lodge of all the genuine lodges in the world was founded in London, and stated that theologians participated in drafting its constitution. Relations with the Church, according to his account, deteriorated in the nineteenth century, with the Enlightenment, the French Revolution, and Italian unification. He also maintained that many clerics, including bishops and cardinals, historically belonged to lodges.
 His thesis clashes with the position of the Holy See, reaffirmed three years ago. In November 2023, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, in a response signed by Cardinal Victor Manuel Fernández and approved by Francis, replied to the Filipino bishop of Dumaguete, Julito Cortes, that the active membership of a faithful in Freemasonry is prohibited due to the incompatibility between Catholic doctrine and Freemasonry, and that those who join it formally and consciously are subject to the provisions of the 1983 declaration. That text, signed by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger as prefect of the then Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and approved by Saint John Paul II, established that the faithful who join Masonic associations are in a state of grave sin .
 Weninger’s argument plays on a legal nuance. The 1917 Code of Canon Law expressly condemned Freemasonry and punished its members with excommunication, while the 1983 Code removed that explicit mention. Ratzinger’s declaration was published precisely to clarify that the change in the Code did not alter the Church’s negative judgment, and the 2023 response confirmed it without distinguishing between regular and irregular lodges.
 Weninger, widowed since 2011, was ordained a priest by Cardinal Christoph Schönborn, now Archbishop Emeritus of Vienna. His thesis on reconciliation between the Church and regular Freemasonry was published in 2019 by the Pontifical Gregorian University. It is not the first time he has presented it publicly: in June 2025 he defended the compatibility between the two, dressed in a cassock, from the podium of the Grande Loge Nationale Française in Paris.
 The issue has echoes in Spain, where it has become known that, while Octavi Vilà was abbot of Poblet and now Archbishop of Barcelona, the Supreme Council of the 33rd Degree gathered its Freemasons in the monastery for three days in June 2017.
 Weninger says that 1.4 million Catholics are in lodges and not excommunicated; Rome recalls that their membership is grave sin.
